must_not_infer: Do not claim remote work is universally harmful or universally beneficial.
Do not invent additional HR metrics, retention numbers, productivity gains, or diversity statistics.
Do not present diversity as a quota-only issue or as unrelated to management systems.
Do not treat one study as proof that all remote work should be reduced or eliminated.
Do not turn policy guidance into legal or HR compliance advice.
must_preserve: Remote work policy sources emphasize clear expectations, tools, communication, performance measurement, and periodic review.
Diversity claims should remain distinct from remote-work policy claims.
Remote work mental-health evidence includes isolation and distress risks, especially for remote-friendly workers living alone.
The Scientific American study claim involves 588,322 Americans and should stay attributed as research context.
Separate productivity, inclusion, and mental-health signals instead of turning them into one simple workplace trend.
benchmark_expected_behavior.notes: Good evaluation case for separating policy, culture, and research evidence without flattening remote work into a single verdict.
benchmark_expected_behavior.preferred_angle: Future-of-work sources mix policy design, inclusion, and mental health. A useful post should argue for operating systems that handle all three instead of treating remote work as only a perk or productivity tactic.
benchmark_expected_behavior.source_dominance_risk: The loneliness study may dominate the angle and turn the post into an anti-remote-work claim.

evidence_to_use.evidence_text: The article provides a comprehensive guide on creating an effective remote work policy, arguing that such a policy is essential for optimizing employee productivity and well-being in a permanent hybrid work environment. It concludes that clear guidelines and defined expectations can help avoid misunderstandings and promote a healthier work-life balance for remote workers. Ensuring consistent communication, providing appropriate tools, and regularly reviewing the policy are critical for success.

evidence_to_use.evidence_text: The article presents research indicating that the long-term shift to remote work post-pandemic has led to increased feelings of isolation and mental distress among American workers, particularly those in remote-friendly jobs who live alone. The author, Emma Harrington, argues that while remote work offers certain benefits, its adverse effects on mental well-being warrant attention. The conclusion emphasizes the need for strategies to mitigate isolation in remote work environments.
